I basically built an AI-driven asset production workflow for mockups.  The issue I was running into was that AI image tools can create a beautiful mockup, but it’s usually one flattened image. So when you try to move that into Lovable, Figma, Webflow, etc., the tool can’t actually recreate the design because it doesn’t have the individual assets.  So I built an agent flow that does the next step:  1. It analyzes a mockup/screen and extracts all the key visual assets: - backgrounds - characters - icons - decor - UI elements - badges - cards - rewards - ambient details  2. It labels each item as either: - something that should be generated as an image asset, like a character, icon, background, or illustration - or something that should be built as real UI, like buttons, cards, progress bars, containers, and text sections  3. It assigns production-friendly values to each asset: - asset name - category - type tag - status - priority - prompt - variants needed - world/brand it belongs to - unlock stage or lifecycle stage - QA notes - transparent background requirement  4. Then it generates the prompts needed to create each individual asset in a consistent visual style, so the whole brand/system doesn’t fall apart visually.  5. After that, I built a Notion export skill that converts the output into rows I can paste directly into a Notion asset database.  So now instead of having one pretty mockup that a builder can’t reproduce, I have an actual asset production pipeline: mockup → asset extraction → UI vs image classification → prompt generation → Notion tracking → asset generation → Figma/Lovable/dev implementation.  It basically turns a flat AI mockup into a reusable design/asset system that can support the full product lifecycle.

Notion is the production system. I set it up with different views so I can actually manage the workflow instead of getting overwhelmed:  * “To Create” → assets that still need prompts or generation * “Prompt Ready” → ready to send to image gen * “Generating” → currently being created * “Needs Fix” → QA issues or style inconsistencies * “Approved” → final assets ready for use * “By World” → grouped by ecosystem  * “Progression Map” → sorted by unlock stage so I can see how assets map to the user journey

Inspired by [From Lovable App to Mobile PWA: Push Notifications with Supabase](https://www.originalobjective.com/blog/from-lovable-app-to-mobile-pwa-push-notifications-with-supabase) by Matt Perry.  ---  ## A Quick Vocabulary Check  Before the steps, here are the words that kept showing up. Plain-language definitions first, technical detail second.  - **PWA (Progressive Web App)** — A regular website that can be "installed" onto a phone's home screen and behave like a real app: its own icon, full screen, and the ability to receive push notifications. - **Service Worker** — A tiny background script the browser keeps running even when your app's tab is closed. Think of it as a quiet helper that listens for messages from the server and shows notifications. Without one, push notifications cannot exist. - **Push Subscription** — A unique "mailbox address" the browser hands you when a user agrees to notifications. You save this address in your database so your server knows where to deliver future messages. - **Edge Function** — A small piece of server code that runs on demand. In this project, it's the bit that actually fires the push out to the browser's mailbox. - **VAPID Keys** — see below, this one deserves its own section.  ### What on earth is a VAPID key?  VAPID stands for **Voluntary Application Server Identification**. The name is ugly, the idea is simple.  When your server sends a push notification, it doesn't talk directly to the user's phone. It talks to a push service run by Google, Apple, or Mozilla, and asks them to deliver the message. Those companies need to know the request is coming from a real, identifiable app and not a spammer.  VAPID is the ID badge.  You generate **two keys** that are mathematically linked:  - **Public key** — lives in the browser. It's baked into your frontend code. When the user subscribes to notifications, this key is part of the "mailbox address" the browser creates. It tells the push service, "messages tagged with this key are allowed to reach me." - **Private key** — lives only on your server, hidden in environment variables. Every time your server sends a push, it signs the request with this key. The push service checks the signature against the public key the user already registered, and if they match, the message gets delivered.  If the keys don't match, the push service refuses to deliver. That's the whole security model.  You generate the pair once, save them, and never change them. Rotating them invalidates every existing subscription, which means every user has to opt in again. So: generate, store carefully, leave alone.  ---  ## The Steps (and the Prompts Behind Them)  ### Step 1 — Lay the Plumbing  **What happened:** Set up the service worker, generated the VAPID keypair, stored the keys as secrets, created a `push_subscriptions` table, and built an Edge Function that can send a push to one user or to everyone.  **What I asked for:**  > "Add real push notifications to the PWA. Generate VAPID keys and store the private key as a secret. Create a `push_subscriptions` table tied to user_id with RLS so users can only see their own. Register a service worker that handles the `push` event and shows the notification. Build a `send-push-notification` Edge Function that takes an optional `user_ids` array — if it's omitted, broadcast to every opted-in user."  **What I'd write today (the better prompt):**  > "Build the full push notification stack for this Lovable PWA in one pass: service worker registration, VAPID keypair (private key as a Cloud secret, public key exposed to the client), a `push_subscriptions` table with RLS, an `unsubscribe` flow that cleans up dead subscriptions, and a `send-push-notification` Edge Function that accepts an optional `user_ids` array (omit = broadcast). Skip backwards-compatibility shims; this is greenfield. Confirm the service worker file is served from the site root, not nested, so its scope covers the whole app."  The "served from the root" line is the one I missed the first time. Service workers can only control pages at or below their own URL, so a worker at `/sw.js` controls everything; one at `/assets/sw.js` controls almost nothing.  ---  ### Step 2 — Pick a Rollout Strategy  **What happened:** Decided new users would default to **opted-in** at the database level, but still see a friendly browser-permission prompt the first time they land on the app. The database flag and the browser permission are two separate things; both need to be "yes" for a push to actually arrive.  **What I asked for:**  > "Default `push_notifications_enabled` to true for new profiles, but show a one-time opt-in modal so the browser permission gets requested in a context the user understands."  **What I'd write today:**  > "Two-layer opt-in: profile flag defaults to true so the user is reachable from day one, plus a one-time modal that explains *why* before triggering the browser's native permission prompt. Persist the 'seen' state in localStorage under a versioned key like `bodtea.pushOptInPrompt.v1` so I can re-trigger the prompt later by bumping the version if I ever need to."  The two layers matter because the browser permission is sticky. If the user clicks "Block" by accident, no amount of database flags will fix it. Asking inside a modal that explains the value first dramatically raises the "Allow" rate.  ---  ### Step 3 — Stop the Popup Showing Every Time  **What happened:** First version re-opened the modal on every page load. Annoying. Fixed by storing a flag in localStorage the moment the user dismisses or accepts.  **What I asked for:**  > "The opt-in popup should only appear once per user per browser. Use localStorage."  **What I'd write today:**  > "Show the opt-in modal at most once per browser, keyed by a versioned localStorage flag. Set the flag on **any** dismissal — accept, deny, or close. Never block app rendering on it; it should appear after the first paint, not before."  Lesson: "show it once" is ambiguous. Be explicit about *when* the flag is set, or you'll see it again every time the user closes it without choosing.  ---  ### Step 4 — Build Real Testing Tools  **What happened:** Added two buttons in Settings. One sends a test push to the current user (everyone gets this one — it's the only honest way to confirm notifications actually work on your specific device). One broadcasts to every opted-in user, locked to the founder's user ID.  **What I asked for:**  > "Add two buttons in Settings: 'Send myself a test push' for any user, and 'Send test push to ALL users' restricted to my user ID. Both call the existing Edge Function."  **What I'd write today:**  > "Settings page needs a personal 'Send test push to myself' button visible to every signed-in user, plus a founder-only broadcast button gated by a server-side check, not just a hidden UI element. The personal test is the most important diagnostic in the app — without it users can't tell if their device is actually receiving pushes."  The "server-side check" detail matters. Hiding a button in the UI based on user ID is fine for UX, but anyone can call an Edge Function directly. The function itself should verify the caller before broadcasting.  ---  ### Step 5 — Show Status in the User's Voice  **What happened:** Added a status line in Settings that combines the database flag and the browser permission into one human sentence in the app's "sis" tone — for example, "✅ You're all set, sis" or "⚠️ Your browser is blocking notifications, sis — here's how to fix it."  **What I asked for:**  > "Show the user's current notification status clearly in Settings. Combine the database flag and `Notification.permission`. Use the 'sis' tone."  **What I'd write today:**  > "Render a single-sentence notification status in Settings that reflects the *true* state: database flag AND `Notification.permission` AND whether a valid push subscription exists. Cover all four combinations explicitly, including the awkward one where the user toggled 'on' in our app but the browser permission is denied. Use the existing brand voice."  Three signals, not two. A user can have the flag on, the browser permission granted, and still have no working subscription if the service worker failed to register. Checking all three keeps "✅ You're all set" from being a lie.  ---  ### Step 6 — Let Users Recover  **What happened:** If the user toggles notifications on in Settings but the browser hasn't granted permission yet, the system clears the localStorage "seen" flag so the opt-in modal can reappear and walk them through it again.  **What I asked for:**  > "If a user enables notifications in Settings but browser permission isn't granted, let the opt-in modal show again."  **What I'd write today:**  > "Treat the Settings toggle as the user *requesting* notifications. If browser permission is `default` or `denied`, clear the localStorage 'seen' flag and re-trigger the opt-in modal so they get a guided path to fixing it. If `denied`, show device-specific instructions instead of just re-asking, because the browser won't prompt twice."  This is the step that turns "broken" into "self-healing." Users almost never know how to undo a "Block" click in their browser settings. Show them.  ---  ## What Made This Successful  Three things, in order of importance:  1. **Asking for the experience, not the API.** "Default users to opted-in but show a one-time modal" got me a thoughtful UX in one shot. "Use the Web Push API" would have got me a wall of code with no opinion behind it. 2. **Treating the database flag and the browser permission as separate facts.** They drift apart constantly, and any feature that assumes they agree will eventually lie to a user. 3. **Building the test buttons early.** I could not have shipped this without the "send myself a test push" button. Reading docs is no substitute for watching a notification land on your own lock screen.  ## The One Prompt I'd Send If I Were Starting Over  > "Add a complete push notification system to this Lovable PWA. Clean up dead subscriptions on send failure. > - New profiles default to `push_notifications_enabled = true`. > - One-time opt-in modal, keyed by versioned localStorage flag, set on any dismissal. Modal explains the value before triggering the native permission prompt. > - Settings page: live status sentence reflecting DB flag + browser permission + subscription presence in the app's brand voice; 'send test push to myself' for everyone; founder-only broadcast button gated server-side; toggling notifications back on from Settings clears the localStorage flag so the modal can re-appear. > - `send-push-notification` Edge Function accepting an optional `user_ids` array (omit = broadcast). > > Use Lovable Cloud for everything. No external services."  That single prompt would have got me to where I am now in a fraction of the back-and-forth.
